title: Hemstitch
subtitle: A drawn-thread stitch that groups exposed warp threads into neat bundles along a hem or border
excerpt: Hemstitch is worked after a band of weft threads has been drawn out of the fabric, leaving bare warp threads exposed. The needle groups those bare threads into small clusters and secures each cluster with a stitch into the solid weave at the edge. The result is a ladder or cluster border used on hems, table linen, and drawn-thread panels.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), drawn thread work chapter. Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), hemstitch and drawn thread entries.

content.text: Hemstitch belongs to drawn-thread work. Before any stitching begins, a set number of weft (horizontal) threads is withdrawn from the fabric across the width of the border, leaving the warp (vertical) threads standing free. The hemstitch needle then travels along the lower edge of this open band, gathering a small group of bare warp threads together with each stitch and locking the group by entering the solid weave below. When the same grouping is repeated along the top edge, the warp threads form a ladder pattern. Working the top groups offset by half creates a zigzag or twist pattern instead.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Fine cotton, coton a broder no. 16 or 25, in a colour matching or slightly darker than the fabric; the grouping stitches should read as neat lines, not as a bold pattern

items.label: Fabric
items.value: Evenweave linen or cotton, 25 to 30 count; withdraw 4 to 6 weft threads for the open band before starting

items.label: Needle
items.value: Tapestry needle size 24 (blunt) so the needle passes between the bare warp threads without splitting them

items.label: Hoop
items.value: Slate frame or scroll frame preferred to keep the withdrawn area taut; a hoop can distort the open band

content.text: Withdraw the weft threads. Using a sharp needle or stiletto, loosen and draw out the required number of weft threads (typically 4 to 6) across the full width of the border. Trim or darn the loose ends into the fabric margin. The remaining warp threads hang free in the open band.

Secure the working thread in the solid weave at the lower edge of the open band, on the wrong side. Bring the needle up through the solid weave at the lower edge, just to the left of the first group of warp threads.

Count the warp threads for the first group (3 or 4 is typical). Pass the needle from right to left behind that group without piercing the fabric, then bring the needle forward. This encircles the bundle. Pull the thread firmly so the group draws together.

Insert the needle into the solid weave immediately to the right of the grouped bundle, at the lower edge of the open band. Bring it up again at the start position for the next group. This locking stitch ties the bundle to the solid edge. Repeat for each group across the row.

For a ladder hemstitch, work the top edge grouping the same bundles together. For a zigzag or Italian hemstitch, group the top edge so each cluster takes half its threads from one lower bundle and half from the next, creating a twist between the two rows.

items.symptom: Groups are uneven and some bundles are wider than others
items.cause: The warp thread count per group was not kept consistent.
items.fix: Count the same number of warp threads for every group before drawing the encircling loop. Mark the boundary with a pin if it helps keep track.

items.symptom: The open band puckers after working the lower edge
items.cause: The locking stitch into the solid weave was pulled too tightly, or the fabric was not mounted taut.
items.fix: Use a consistent, moderate tension rather than a tight one. The warp threads should draw together but the fabric edge should remain flat. A rigid frame rather than a hoop helps hold the band open.

items.symptom: Weft threads are difficult to withdraw evenly
items.cause: The fabric count is very fine or the weave is stiffened with dressing.
items.fix: Wash and press the fabric before working to remove any dressing. Use a stiletto or pin to loosen the first thread at one selvedge, then draw it out slowly with tweezers or your fingers.

content.text: Hemstitch is the main stitch for drawn-thread borders on household linen, such as tablecloths, napkins, and shirt cuffs. It often pairs with
, which makes its open holes by tension rather than by pulling threads out.
